newsitem.title: UK: Guinness rejects reports of brand divestment.
newsitem.headline: Guinness rejects reports of brand divestment.

text.p: British drinks group Guinness Plc has no plans to streamline brands as a result of its proposed merger with Grand Metropolitian Plc, a spokesman for the company said on Sunday.
"There are no plans to streamline any brands...no secret plans to divest," he told Reuters.

Newspaper reports on Sunday had speculated that the merged group, to be called GMG Brands, would either decide to ditch some of its combined spirits portfolio to rationalise brands in order to ease marketing or would shed brands to pacify regulators.

"We are confident that we can properly explain to regulators...that the proposed merger does not bring competition or regulatory problems. So (the reports) are all speculation and we would not comment," the spokesman said.
Guinness and Grand Met unveiled the 23 billion pound ($37.6 billion) merger, the biggest in British corporate history, on May 12.
It will create the world's leading spirits and wine company and the group will be the world's seventh largest branded food and drinks concern.

Guinness chairman Tony Greener told shareholders at the annual meeting on May 15 that "the range of brands are highly complementary," adding that both groups had remarkably different brands with very few overlaps.
Greener said the merged group would represent about five percent of the world spirits market and that the board was confident the merger would be cleared.
The Sunday Times newspaper said brands which could be divested were thought to include VAT 69, while the Independent on Sunday highlighted Dewar's whisky as likely to be under threat in the U.S.

The Independent on Sunday added that gin brand Tanqueray's looked the most likely candidate for disposal if the merged group's gin operations -- which include brands such as Gordon's, Gilbey's and Bombay Sapphire -- were required to shed interests.

The planned merger has drawn complaints from rival Seagram Co Ltd, which described it as anti-competitive, while Allied Domecq has set up a task force to look at whether the merger would have an unfair dominance in any of its markets.
Some investors have taken a view that Allied now looks weak and in dire need of strategic partners if it is to stop its market share being eroded.
The Observer suggested Seagram was the most likely partner for Allied, with Bacardi, Brown-Forman, Jim Beam Brands and Pernod Ricard all possible contenders.
The merger between Guinness and Grand Met could also trigger a valuation of all the new group's brands, which could double the current stated value, the Sunday Business newspaper said.
It said Guinness, the company's famous stout, was likely to be valued at around one billion pounds.
The newspaper quoted Grand Met saying that "brand values are very important to the two companies and will be clearly stated."
